unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Redmire Snack Foods is a private limited company in Country X that produces savoury snack packs. It sells 240,000 packs a year at $1.80 each, generating $432,000 in revenue, and employs 35 staff. Its founder, Priya Raman, started the firm 9 years ago and sales have been flat for 18 months. A multinational company from Country Z, Nordvik Foods, wants Redmire to become a dedicated supplier to its new Country X distribution centre.

Nordvik Foods proposes a 3-year contract for 300,000 packs a year at $1.45 per pack, requiring Redmire to invest $90,000 in a new packing line and pass quality audits four times a year. The Country X government offers firms in development regions a grant covering 20% of machinery costs. Redmire must decide whether to accept the contract or keep supplying domestic retailers at current prices.

questions.question_text: Define 'host country'.
questions.model_answer: The country in which a multinational company locates production, offices or sales operations, which is different from the country where the multinational was originally based [2].

knowledge_max_2: a multinational locates production/sales/operations in another country
that country is different from the multinational's home/origin country

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Redmire Snack Foods of accepting the Nordvik Foods contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A 3-year deal gives Redmire predictable, large-scale orders [k], with Nordvik wanting 300,000 packs a year, 60,000 more than the 240,000 packs Redmire currently sells [app]. Benefit 2: The government grant cuts the cost of the new packing line [k], covering 20% of the $90,000 investment, a saving of $18,000 [app].

knowledge_max_2: guaranteed/regular large orders / stable demand from the multinational
government grants/support reduce the cost of investment
application_max_2: 300,000 packs a year vs 240,000 packs currently (60,000 more)
20% grant on $90,000 = $18,000 saving on the packing line

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Redmire Snack Foods could face if it accepts the Nordvik Foods contract.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The contract price is much lower [k], at $1.45 per pack versus $1.80 for domestic retailers [app], so revenue per pack falls by about 19% and profits may shrink unless Redmire raises output efficiency [an]. Problem 2: Redmire could become too dependent on one buyer [k], because Nordvik's 300,000 packs would exceed Redmire's entire current output of 240,000 [app], leaving Redmire vulnerable if Nordvik ends the 3-year deal or demands price cuts later [an].

knowledge_max_2: lower contract prices squeeze profit margins
over-dependence on a single customer/buyer
application_max_2: $1.45 per pack vs $1.80 domestic (about 19% lower)
300,000 packs would exceed all current output of 240,000 packs
analysis_max_2: profits shrink unless efficiency/output rises to offset lower prices
vulnerable if the 3-year contract ends or prices are renegotiated downward

questions.question_text: Do you think Redmire Snack Foods should accept the Nordvik Foods contract or keep supplying domestic retailers at current prices? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the contract gives Redmire predictable, high-volume sales [k], with 300,000 packs at $1.45 bringing in $435,000 a year, close to the $432,000 it earns domestically now [app], and the 20% grant saves $18,000 on the $90,000 packing line, so unit costs should fall as volume rises [an]. However, the price is well below the $1.80 domestic rate [k], so Redmire must check that higher volumes still cover costs and the four quality audits a year [app]; failing an audit could lose the 3-year deal after Redmire has committed $72,000 of its own money [an]. On balance, Redmire should accept the contract, because secured volume growth and the grant outweigh the margin risk for a firm whose sales have been flat for 18 months [eval]; it should also keep some domestic retail sales so no single buyer ever dominates [eval].

knowledge_max_2: multinational contracts offer large, predictable volumes and scale
lower prices and single-buyer dependence are risks of such deals
application_max_2: $1.80 domestic vs $1.45 contract price; four quality audits a year; flat sales for 18 months
analysis_max_2: economies of scale and falling unit costs from higher output and the grant
margin risk and audit failure could strand the $72,000 investment
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on accepting the contract or not
recognises the continuing value of domestic retail sales as diversification

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Wharfdale Cement Co is a private limited company in Country X, close to the northern quarry belt. It produced 180,000 tonnes of cement last year at a cost of $38 a tonne and sells at $52 a tonne, employing 64 workers. Domestic demand has grown slowly, at about 3% a year, and imports from Country Z have undercut its prices.

The directors are weighing two options: invest $2.4 million in a grinding plant in Country Y, where construction is booming and labour is 30% cheaper, or spend $1.1 million upgrading the Country X plant to export through the southern port. Country Y demand is projected at 400,000 tonnes a year, but the project needs a skilled expatriate team for the first 2 years and carries political and currency risks.

questions.question_text: Outline one benefit to a business of becoming a multinational company.
questions.model_answer: It can access larger markets abroad, increasing sales and spreading risk across countries rather than relying on one domestic economy [2].

knowledge_max_2: access to larger/more foreign markets
spreads risk / less dependence on the home economy

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Wharfdale Cement Co of building the Country Y plant.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A Country Y plant would give Wharfdale access to a much bigger market [k], where projected demand is 400,000 tonnes a year, more than double its current 180,000 tonnes in Country X [app]. Benefit 2: Producing locally in Country Y would cut costs [k], because labour there is 30% cheaper, widening the $14 margin on each $52 tonne sold [app].

knowledge_max_2: access to larger foreign markets / more customers
lower operating costs from cheaper labour/inputs
application_max_2: 400,000 tonnes projected demand vs 180,000 tonnes produced now
labour 30% cheaper in Country Y; cost $38 vs price $52

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Wharfdale Cement Co could face if it builds the Country Y plant.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The overseas plant demands heavy capital [k], at $2.4 million versus just $1.1 million for the export-upgrade option [app], so cash is tied up for years and any fall in Country Y demand would sharply reduce returns [an]. Problem 2: Operating abroad brings unfamiliar risks [k], including the 2 years of expatriate management and the political risks the board foresees [app], which could disrupt production and make budgeting very difficult [an].

knowledge_max_2: very high capital cost / large upfront investment
unfamiliar country risks (political, currency, management)
application_max_2: $2.4 million for Country Y vs $1.1 million for export upgrade
2 years expatriate team; political and currency risks noted by the board
analysis_max_2: capital tied up; a fall in Country Y demand cuts returns
disruption risk and difficult budgeting in an unfamiliar country

questions.question_text: Do you think Wharfdale Cement Co should build the Country Y plant or upgrade the Country X plant for export? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building in Country Y would let Wharfdale capture 400,000 tonnes of projected demand right at the customer [k], helped by 30% cheaper labour and the booming construction market [app], raising margins on each $52 tonne and spreading risk across two countries [an]. However, it costs $2.4 million, more than double the $1.1 million export upgrade [k], and needs 2 years of expatriate managers with political and currency risks [app], so a downturn in Country Y construction could leave an idle plant and stretched cash flow [an]. On balance, Wharfdale should upgrade the Country X plant and export through the southern port first [eval], because it is cheaper, reversible and tests overseas demand using existing strengths [eval].

knowledge_max_2: multinational location in growth markets brings scale and lower costs
overseas investment carries heavy capital and country risks
application_max_2: 400,000 tonnes projected demand; 30% cheaper labour; $52 per tonne
$2.4 million vs $1.1 million export option; 2 years expatriate team
analysis_max_2: higher margins and risk spreading via Country Y production
idle-plant/cash-flow risk if Country Y demand falters; export route is reversible
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (export first vs Y plant)
recognises staged/conditional logic: revisit Country Y after export proves demand

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Dunharrow Woollen Mills is a private limited company in Country X that weaves woollen cloth for suit makers. It produces 60,000 metres a month, employs 110 weavers and exports 25% of output. Country X has removed most trade barriers on textile imports and signed tariff-cutting deals with 9 countries, and improved container shipping has cut delivery times to overseas buyers from 6 weeks to 10 days.

A tailoring group in Country Y has offered to buy 1.2 million metres a year if Dunharrow can weave to its specification within 12 months. Dunharrow could either export from Country X or discuss a joint venture to weave in Country Y. The owner, Marcus Whitfield, fears the Country Y partner may copy designs, but keeping all production at home limits how fast the order can be served.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A government-imposed restriction on international trade, such as a tariff (tax on imports) or a quota (limit on the quantity of imports), used to protect domestic industry [2].

knowledge_max_2: a government-imposed restriction on international trade
examples include tariffs (import taxes) and quotas

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities that the removal of trade barriers has created for Dunharrow Woollen Mills.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Lower trade barriers open larger export markets [k], and the Country Y tailoring group alone wants 1.2 million metres a year, far more than the 60,000 metres Dunharrow makes each month [app]. Opportunity 2: Faster, cheaper shipping widens Dunharrow's reach [k], because delivery times have fallen from 6 weeks to 10 days, making overseas orders practical [app].

knowledge_max_2: access to larger foreign markets after barriers removed
improved transport/communications make global trade faster and cheaper
application_max_2: 1.2 million metres a year wanted by Country Y vs 60,000 metres a month made
delivery times cut from 6 weeks to 10 days; deals with 9 countries

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Dunharrow Woollen Mills could face if it forms the joint venture with the Country Y partner.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Dunharrow risks losing its designs [k], because the Country Y partner would see its specification and could copy it once the 12 months are up [app], damaging Dunharrow's competitive advantage in woven cloth [an]. Problem 2: A joint venture splits control [k], so decisions about quality, output and price must be agreed with the partner [app], which can slow responses to faults and disappoint the tailoring group [an].

knowledge_max_2: risk of ideas/designs being copied by the partner
shared control slows decisions and creates friction
application_max_2: specification visible to partner; risk after the 12 months agreement
shared decisions on quality, output and price versus 1.2 million metres commitment
analysis_max_2: losing design secrecy destroys Dunharrow's competitive advantage
slower quality/fault responses risk breaching the order's standards

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunharrow Woollen Mills should serve the Country Y order by exporting from Country X or by forming the joint venture? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting from Country X keeps Dunharrow in full control of its designs and quality [k], letting it earn the whole margin on 1.2 million metres a year through the 10-day container route [app], protecting the jobs of its 110 weavers and avoiding the risk of a partner copying its work [an]. Forming the joint venture would share the cost of weaving to specification and speed up the ramp-up within 12 months [k], giving local knowledge but splitting profits and ceding control of quality and price decisions [app], with the real danger of a future competitor armed with Dunharrow's specification [an]. On balance, Dunharrow should export from Country X [eval], because design protection and full margins outweigh shared setup costs, accepting a tight 12-month capacity challenge [eval].

knowledge_max_2: exporting keeps full control and captures full profit
joint ventures share cost/resources but split control and profits
application_max_2: 1.2 million metres a year; 10-day container route; 110 weavers; 25% exports
12-month deadline to weave to specification; Country Y partner demands
analysis_max_2: design secrecy and full margins vs partner copying and shared profits
capacity strain under 12-month deadline vs faster local ramp-up
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between exporting and the joint venture
weighs design protection/margin against speed and shared cost

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Stormont Electronics Ltd is a public limited company in Country X that assembles set-top boxes and routers. Its subsidiary in Country Z employs 480 workers and earned $6.2 million profit last year, of which $4.5 million was repatriated to Country X and $1.7 million was kept in Country Z as retained profit. The Country Z government has criticised foreign firms for moving profits home.

The board must decide whether to repatriate $5 million of this year's expected $6.8 million subsidiary profit to pay a special dividend in Country X, or reinvest it in a new assembly hall in Country Z costing $5.5 million. The Country X parent needs funds to upgrade its own factory, while the Country Z government hints that firms reinvesting locally may receive preferential tax treatment.

questions.question_text: Define 'repatriation of profits'.
questions.model_answer: The transfer of profits earned by a multinational's subsidiary or branch in a foreign country back to the parent company in its home country [2].

knowledge_max_2: profits earned abroad are returned to the home/parent company
typically by a multinational's subsidiary or branch

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for Country Z of Stormont repatriating $5 million of subsidiary profits.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Country Z loses funds that could support local growth [k], because returning $5 million of the $6.8 million expected profit would leave only $1.8 million to reinvest or tax locally [app]. Problem 2: The host country gains less from foreign investment [k], so the planned assembly hall and its construction orders for local suppliers could be postponed [app].

knowledge_max_2: less money remains in the host country for reinvestment
fewer local benefits (jobs, supplier orders, taxes) from the MNC's presence
application_max_2: $5 million repatriated out of $6.8 million expected profit leaves $1.8 million
assembly hall ($5.5 million) postponed / local construction orders lost

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Stormont Electronics Ltd might choose to repatriate the profits to Country X.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Shareholders expect rewards from abroad [k], and paying a special dividend from repatriated profits boosts returns and may support the share price [app], which is why the board lists repatriation despite criticism from Country Z [an]. Reason 2: The parent company urgently needs funds at home [k], so repatriating $5 million could part-finance the Country X factory upgrade without new borrowing [app], improving productivity where head office and most owners are based [an].

knowledge_max_2: reward shareholders / pay dividends
fund home-country investment without borrowing
application_max_2: special dividend planned to be paid in Country X
$5 million earmarked toward the Country X factory upgrade
analysis_max_2: shareholder approval and share-price support despite host-country criticism
improved home productivity / avoids interest on new loans

questions.question_text: Do you think Stormont Electronics Ltd should repatriate $5 million or reinvest it in the Country Z assembly hall? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Repatriating $5 million rewards shareholders and helps fund the Country X factory upgrade [k], continuing last year's pattern of sending $4.5 million home while keeping $1.7 million locally [app], though taking $5 million of the expected $6.8 million could worsen relations with the Country Z government and invite punitive taxes [an]. Reinvesting $5.5 million in the Country Z hall would secure the 480 workers' jobs, win the hinted preferential tax treatment and expand capacity near the market [k], but it leaves the Country X factory underfunded and Country X shareholders without their special dividend [app], tying scarce cash to one overseas site that faces political risk [an]. On balance, Stormont should reinvest in the assembly hall [eval], because the tax preference and host-country goodwill are worth more than this year's dividend, provided the board explains the decision clearly to shareholders [eval].

knowledge_max_2: repatriation rewards shareholders and funds the parent company
reinvestment secures host-country relations, jobs and possible tax benefits
application_max_2: $4.5 million sent home vs $1.7 million retained in Country Z last year
$5 million vs $5.5 million hall; $6.8 million expected profit; special dividend
analysis_max_2: risk of punitive taxes and worsened host-country relations from heavy repatriation
shareholder disappointment/underfunded home factory vs tax preference and job security
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (reinvest vs repatriate)
recognises need to manage shareholder expectations alongside the decision

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making brake discs and hub assemblies for domestic vehicle assemblers. It employs 88 workers, sells 500,000 discs a year and had revenue of $9.6 million last year, growing at about 8% a year. A foreign multinational, Kestrel Mobility Group, is opening a vehicle assembly plant in Country X and wants Trevelyan to supply 700,000 discs annually under a 4-year deal.

To win the contract Trevelyan must install automated grinding equipment costing $800,000 and meet Kestrel's quality standard, which Kestrel's engineers would help install. Trevelyan was founded by Diane Trevelyan 14 years ago and could instead stay with its domestic customers, who buy 300,000 discs a year at higher prices, but growth would remain slow.

questions.question_text: Define 'technology transfer'.
questions.model_answer: The movement of technology, such as equipment, knowledge or skills, from one business or country to another, often from a multinational to a local business in the host country [2].

knowledge_max_2: technology/knowledge/skills move between businesses or countries
often flows from a multinational to a local firm or host country

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd of winning the Kestrel contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The contract would sharply increase Trevelyan's sales [k], with Kestrel wanting 700,000 discs a year against 500,000 currently made and 300,000 bought by domestic customers [app]. Benefit 2: Trevelyan gains new technology and skills [k], because Kestrel's engineers would help install the $800,000 automated grinding equipment, lifting quality and productivity [app].

knowledge_max_2: much larger sales volume / access to a bigger customer
access to modern technology and skills (technology transfer)
application_max_2: 700,000 discs a year vs 500,000 current output / 300,000 domestic sales
Kestrel engineers help install the $800,000 automated grinding equipment

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd could face from the Kestrel deal.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The deal demands heavy investment [k], with $800,000 of equipment against domestic sales of only 300,000 discs a year [app], so Trevelyan must borrow or use savings and risks losses if Kestrel cuts the order [an]. Problem 2: Trevelyan could become dependent on one customer [k], because 700,000 discs a year for 4 years would dominate its output [app], leaving it exposed if Kestrel switches supplier or closes the plant later [an].

knowledge_max_2: high capital cost requiring loans or savings
over-dependence on a single large customer
application_max_2: $800,000 equipment vs domestic sales of 300,000 discs a year
700,000 discs a year for 4 years would dominate output
analysis_max_2: debt/savings drain and losses if the order is cut or delayed
single-buyer exposure; plant closure or supplier switch would be devastating

questions.question_text: Do you think Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd should accept the Kestrel contract or keep supplying domestic customers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the Kestrel deal offers 700,000 discs a year of secured sales, well above Trevelyan's 500,000 output, plus technology transfer as Kestrel's engineers help install the grinding equipment [k]; the $800,000 cost is steep, but the 4-year contract spreads it and domestic demand of 300,000 discs cannot fill the line alone [app], so productivity and worker skills should jump [an]. Staying with domestic customers keeps higher prices and avoids $800,000 of debt [k], but growth stays slow and Trevelyan may lose competitiveness as rivals modernise [app], eventually shrinking its $9.6 million revenue [an]. On balance, Trevelyan should accept the contract [eval], because the scale, skills and technology gains outweigh the dependence risk, provided it keeps some domestic buyers for diversification [eval].

knowledge_max_2: MNC contracts bring volume, technology and skills to local firms
dependence and capital risk accompany a single large buyer
application_max_2: 700,000 discs vs 500,000 output and 300,000 domestic demand
$800,000 equipment; 4-year contract; $9.6 million revenue at stake
analysis_max_2: productivity and skills gains from technology transfer vs debt burden
domestic stability but falling competitiveness if rivals modernise first
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (accept vs stay domestic)
recognises keeping some domestic buyers as a hedge/condition

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brentmoor Steel Plc is a public limited company in Country X producing steel rods and sheet for construction firms. It employs 320 workers, makes 90,000 tonnes a year at a cost of $540 a tonne and sells at $610. Cheap imported steel from Country Z, priced about 18% below Brentmoor's price, has cut its domestic market share from 30% to 22% in 2 years.

Country X's government is consulting on a 15% import tariff on foreign steel, which would raise import prices and shield local mills. Brentmoor's largest customers, two construction groups, oppose the tariff because it raises their building costs. The board must decide whether to lobby for the tariff or compete without protection by cutting its $540 cost per tonne.

questions.question_text: Define 'protectionism'.
questions.model_answer: Government policies that shield domestic industries from foreign competition, for example by imposing tariffs (import taxes) or quotas (limits on import quantities) [2].

knowledge_max_2: policies that shield domestic industries from imports
e.g. tariffs on imports or quotas

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Brentmoor Steel Plc of Country X imposing the 15% import tariff.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: A tariff makes imported steel more expensive [k], narrowing the 18% price gap beneath Brentmoor's $610 and helping it win back market share from 22% [app]. Advantage 2: Protected demand would let Brentmoor use capacity fully [k], with its 90,000 tonnes a year and 320 workers better utilised rather than cutting shifts [app].

knowledge_max_2: imports become pricier; domestic goods more price-competitive
protected demand raises capacity utilisation and protects jobs
application_max_2: 18% price gap closed vs $610; market share fell to 22%
90,000 tonnes a year and 320 workers better utilised

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of the proposed tariff for Brentmoor Steel Plc's stakeholders.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Construction customers would oppose Brentmoor [k], since the 15% import tariff raises their steel costs above the current $610 market price [app], risking lost orders to overseas contractors and damaged relationships [an]. Problem 2: Protection can reduce pressure to improve [k], so Brentmoor might delay cutting its $540 cost per tonne [app], leaving it weak if the tariff is later removed by trade deals [an].

knowledge_max_2: customers/consumers face higher input costs and oppose protection
protection reduces the incentive to raise efficiency
application_max_2: two construction groups oppose; tariff lifts costs above $610
$540 cost per tonne pressure; 18% import price gap
analysis_max_2: lost orders to overseas contractors; strained customer relationships
complacency / vulnerable if the tariff is later removed

questions.question_text: Do you think Brentmoor Steel Plc should lobby for the tariff or compete without protection by cutting costs? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Lobbying for the 15% tariff would narrow the 18% import gap, lifting Brentmoor's $610 competitiveness and defending its 22% market share and 320 workers [k], but it risks alienating the two construction groups that buy much of its 90,000 tonnes a year and invites retaliation against Country X exporters [app], while discouraging the efficiency drive needed on the $540 cost [an]. Cutting costs to compete freely keeps customers loyal and prepares Brentmoor for any removal of protection [k], but trimming $540 per tonne below import prices 18% under $610 is hard and may mean wage or job cuts [app], with no guarantee of success [an]. On balance, Brentmoor should lobby for the tariff in the short term while committing to an internal efficiency programme [eval], because defending 320 jobs now matters and protection cannot be permanent [eval].

knowledge_max_2: tariffs protect domestic industry from cheaper imports
protection raises customer costs and breeds complacency
application_max_2: 15% tariff vs 18% import gap; $540 cost and $610 price; 22% share
two construction groups oppose; 90,000 tonnes a year; 320 workers
analysis_max_2: tariff defends jobs/share but risks losing customers and retaliation
efficiency focus keeps loyalty but is hard and may cut wages/jobs
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified position (short-term lobbying with long-term efficiency)
recognises protection is temporary, not permanent

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Solway Preserves Co is a private limited company in Country X making jars of jam and chutney. It produces 800,000 jars a year, employs 46 staff and exports 15% of output. Jam accounts for 62% of jars sold. Improved container shipping and online ordering have opened markets abroad: Solway now receives enquiries from supermarkets in 6 countries and from customers via social media adverts reaching 2 million people.

The owners are weighing two options: invest $150,000 in a larger filling line to double output for export orders, or keep production at its current level and sell more in Country X, where two rivals have recently launched discount jams. Solway's cash reserves stand at $220,000 and the bank has offered a loan at 9% interest for expansion.

questions.question_text: Identify two reasons for globalisation.
questions.model_answer: Improvements in transport and communications technology, making international trade faster and cheaper; the removal or reduction of trade barriers such as tariffs and quotas [2].

knowledge_max_2: improvements in transport/communications (e.g. container shipping, internet)
removal/reduction of trade barriers such as tariffs or quotas

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why globalisation is creating opportunities for Solway Preserves Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Cheaper, faster transport lets Solway reach distant buyers [k], and supermarkets in 6 countries have already enquired about importing its jars [app]. Reason 2: The internet and global media spread product awareness [k], with Solway's social media adverts reaching 2 million people and pulling in overseas interest [app].

knowledge_max_2: improved transport/communication opens export markets
global media/internet spread brand awareness worldwide
application_max_2: enquiries from supermarkets in 6 countries
social media adverts reaching 2 million people

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Solway Preserves Co could face if it doubles production for export.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Doubling output needs heavy spending [k], with $150,000 for the bigger filling line on top of $220,000 reserves and a 9% loan [app], so interest and repayments strain cash if export orders lag [an]. Problem 2: Overseas buyers may demand changes [k], such as different labels, recipes or health regulations [app], raising costs and risking rejected shipments [an].

knowledge_max_2: high expansion cost financed by reserves or loans
foreign markets demand adaptation (labels, tastes, regulations)
application_max_2: $150,000 line vs $220,000 reserves and a 9% loan offer
enquiries from 6 countries with differing requirements
analysis_max_2: interest/repayment strain if export orders arrive slowly
higher adaptation costs and risk of rejected shipments

questions.question_text: Do you think Solway Preserves Co should invest in the new filling line to double output for export, or keep production the same and sell more in Country X? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing $150,000 would let Solway exploit enquiries from 6 countries and its reach to 2 million people on social media, doubling 800,000 jars of annual production [k]; with $220,000 reserves and a 9% loan, the line is affordable, and it would grow exports beyond the current 15% of output [app], spreading risk beyond a home market under attack from two discount rivals [an]. Keeping production steady avoids debt and the risk of unsold jars if overseas buyers prove slow [k], but it blocks growth and leaves Solway fighting discount jams at home with stagnant margins [app], likely losing share in Country X as well [an]. On balance, Solway should invest in the filling line [eval], taking the 9% loan only if confirmed export orders cover the repayments comfortably [eval].

knowledge_max_2: globalisation opens overseas demand through transport and media
expansion financed by reserves/loans carries repayment risk
application_max_2: $150,000 line; $220,000 reserves; 9% loan; 6 countries; 2 million reach
two discount rivals at home; exports at 15%; 800,000 jars a year
analysis_max_2: risk spreading beyond the embattled home market vs export order risk
domestic price war undermines the stand-still strategy
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (invest vs stay at current output)
conditional logic: loan only when confirmed orders cover repayments

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Fenwick Wind Components Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing steel towers and nacelles for wind turbines. It employs 74 workers, makes 120 towers a year and has revenue of $14 million. The Country X government has introduced local content rules requiring at least 45% of the value of every wind farm project to be made by Country X firms.

NordAero, a multinational turbine maker, plans a $30 million turbine plant in Country X and has asked Fenwick to become its local content supplier for 200 towers a year under a 5-year deal. Fenwick would need $3.2 million for new pressing equipment and would rely on NordAero for 80% of its revenue. Its alternative is to serve existing domestic customers, who order 90 towers a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'local content rules'.
questions.model_answer: Government rules requiring that a minimum share of a product's value or materials be made in the host country, used to boost domestic industry and jobs [2].

knowledge_max_2: rules requiring a minimum share of a product to be made locally
used to boost host-country industry/employment

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Fenwick Wind Components Ltd of supplying the NordAero plant.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The deal would more than double Fenwick's output [k], with NordAero wanting 200 towers a year against 120 made now and only 90 ordered by domestic customers [app]. Advantage 2: Five years of contracted orders give Fenwick stable demand [k], supporting investment in the new pressing equipment and protecting the jobs of its 74 workers [app].

knowledge_max_2: much larger orders / rapid output growth
long-term stable contracts aid planning and investment
application_max_2: 200 towers a year wanted vs 120 made now and 90 domestic orders
5-year deal; 74 workers; $3.2 million pressing equipment supported

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Fenwick Wind Components Ltd could face if it supplies NordAero.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Fenwick would owe its survival to one buyer [k], because 80% of its revenue would come from NordAero under the 5-year deal [app], so any cancellation or price cut would threaten the whole business [an]. Problem 2: The $3.2 million pressing equipment strains finances [k], especially while relying on NordAero for 80% of revenue [app], so if NordAero's $30 million plant is delayed Fenwick still carries the debt [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Marlowe Bicycles is a private limited company in Country X making steel-framed commuter bicycles. It employs 28 workers, sells 9,000 bicycles a year at $210 and has $1.9 million revenue. Two multinational retailers have entered Country X, selling imported bicycles at $150, and Marlowe's sales fell 20% last year while its market share dropped from 12% to 9%.

Marlowe's founder, Ellis Marlowe, opened the first workshop 14 years ago and the workforce is proud of its hand-built frames. The board must choose between two strategies: cut prices towards $160 and match the imports, or target a niche with hand-made premium touring bikes at $520, aimed at cycling tourists. The premium option needs $120,000 of retooling and specialist welders, but forecasts suggest sales of 800 premium bikes a year initially.

questions.question_text: Identify two threats of globalisation for businesses.
questions.model_answer: Stronger competition from foreign firms and multinationals entering the home market; downward pressure on prices and loss of market share for domestic businesses [2].

knowledge_max_2: increased foreign competition / MNC entry into the domestic market
downward price pressure and loss of market share for local firms

questions.question_text: Explain two ways globalisation is threatening Marlowe Bicycles.
questions.model_answer: Threat 1: Multinational retailers sell imports far cheaper [k], at $150 per bicycle versus Marlowe's $210 [app], forcing painful discounting or lost sales. Threat 2: Globalisation has eroded Marlowe's position [k], with sales down 20% last year and market share falling from 12% to 9% [app].

knowledge_max_2: cheaper imports undercut domestic prices
foreign competition takes sales and market share
application_max_2: $150 imports vs Marlowe's $210 price
sales down 20% last year; market share 12% to 9%

questions.question_text: Explain two possible responses Marlowe Bicycles could take to the multinational threat.
questions.model_answer: Response 1: Cut prices towards $160 [k], close to the $150 imports, which might win back price-sensitive buyers [app], restoring volume at the cost of much thinner margins and possible losses per bicycle [an]. Response 2: Differentiate with premium touring bikes at $520 [k], aimed at cycling tourists untouched by the $150 import flood [app], building loyalty in a niche where 800 bikes a year at higher margins could still profit [an].

knowledge_max_2: competing on price / cost leadership against imports
differentiation / targeting a niche market
application_max_2: $160 close to $150 imports; margins squeezed on each bicycle
$520 premium touring bikes; cycling tourists; 800 bikes a year forecast
analysis_max_2: higher volume but much thinner or negative margins
niche loyalty and higher margins vs smaller total market

questions.question_text: Do you think Marlowe Bicycles should cut prices towards $160 to match imports, or move into premium touring bikes at $520? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Matching imports at $160 might recover volume, but leaves almost no margin against $150 rivals [k], coming after sales already fell 20% and share dropped to 9% [app], so Marlowe could sell more bicycles yet still lose money, endangering its 28 jobs [an]. The premium route targets cycling tourists at $520 [k], needing $120,000 of retooling to sell an initial 800 bikes a year worth about $416,000 at healthy margins [app], avoiding a price war and building a defensible niche [an]. On balance, Marlowe should move into premium touring bikes [eval], because a 9%-share commuter range cannot beat global firms on price against $150 imports [eval].

differentiation avoids head-on price wars with global firms

analysis_max_2: volume recovery with no margin endangers the whole firm and jobs
niche strategy restores profitability and defensibility
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (premium vs price match)
links the recommendation to the 9% market share reality

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Drummond Chocolates Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making handmade truffles and bars. It buys cocoa from Country Y and sells 1.5 million bars a year at $3.50, employing 57 staff with $5.25 million revenue. A new free trade agreement between Country X and its neighbours has removed the 8% tariff on cocoa and on chocolate exports.

Drummond's board must decide whether to build a $1.8 million export factory to sell 2.6 million bars a year across the free trade region, or keep the single factory and rely on premium domestic sales, where it already holds 18% market share. The new factory needs 25 extra workers and two years to reach full capacity, but regional sales could raise annual revenue to $9.1 million.

questions.question_text: Define 'free trade'.
questions.model_answer: International trade between countries without tariffs, quotas or other restrictions, allowing goods and services to cross borders freely [2].

knowledge_max_2: trade between countries without tariffs/quotas/restrictions
goods and services move freely across borders

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities the free trade agreement creates for Drummond Chocolates Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Removing the 8% export tariff makes Drummond's bars cheaper in neighbouring countries [k], supporting sales of up to 2.6 million bars a year across the region [app]. Opportunity 2: Removing the 8% tariff on cocoa cuts Drummond's input costs [k], improving margins on every bar sold at home and in the region [app].

knowledge_max_2: export tariffs removed, so market access is cheaper/easier abroad
input tariffs removed, so production costs fall
application_max_2: 2.6 million bars a year possible under the regional plan
8% tariff gone on cocoa bought from Country Y

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Drummond Chocolates Ltd could face if it builds the export factory.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $1.8 million factory strains finances [k], with only $5.25 million current revenue and two years before full capacity [app], so Drummond may need loans and face heavy interest during the ramp-up [an]. Problem 2: Regional competition is unfamiliar [k], with established local brands and price-sensitive shoppers [app], risking slow sales of the extra bars and wasted capacity [an].

knowledge_max_2: high capital cost with a slow ramp-up creates financing risk
unfamiliar foreign competition and price sensitivity
application_max_2: $1.8 million factory; $5.25 million revenue; two years to full capacity
2.6 million bars a year target vs 1.5 million bars now
analysis_max_2: loan/interest burden during the slow ramp-up period
slow uptake risks wasted capacity and weak returns

questions.question_text: Do you think Drummond Chocolates Ltd should build the export factory for the free trade region, or keep the single factory focused on domestic premium sales? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the export factory exploits free trade: with the 8% tariff gone, Drummond could sell 2.6 million bars a year and lift revenue from $5.25 million to $9.1 million [k], with cocoa also cheaper and 25 extra workers strengthening production [app], achieving larger scale and spreading risk beyond an 18%-share home market [an]. Keeping the single factory avoids $1.8 million of debt and protects the proven premium domestic position [k], but it ignores a revenue rise of about $3.85 million and leaves capacity trapped while regional rivals expand [app], risking long-term decline [an]. On balance, Drummond should build the export factory [eval], staged so the loan is only drawn once confirmed regional orders justify it [eval].

knowledge_max_2: free trade removes tariffs, opening markets and cutting input costs
expansion carries heavy capital cost and ramp-up risk
application_max_2: 8% tariff gone; 2.6 million bars a year; revenue $5.25 million to $9.1 million
$1.8 million factory; two years to capacity; 18% domestic share; 25 extra workers
analysis_max_2: larger scale and risk spreading vs $1.8 million debt and ramp-up risk
ignoring a ~$3.85 million opportunity vs protecting the premium domestic niche
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (build vs stay single factory)
staged/conditional approach tied to confirmed regional orders
